metadata.title: Well Posedness of the Problem of Estimation Fractional Derivative for a Distribution Function.

nodes.name: Nonparametric estimation of the fractional derivative of a distribution function
nodes.statement: {\bf We consider here the problem of the nonparametric estimation of the fractional derivative for a distribution function based on the sample of a "great" volume, and analogously estimation of the fractional derivative of the spectral function of Gaussian stationary sequence. }
nodes.statement_short: Estimate nonparametrically the fractional derivative of an unknown distribution function (and of a spectral function) from a large sample.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Well posedness of fractional-derivative estimation for $\alpha < 1/2$
nodes.statement: We will prove that if the order of the fractional derivative $ \alpha $ is less than 1/2, then these problems are well posed. In particular, the speed of convergence of offered unbiased estimate is $ 1/\sqrt{n}, $ as in the case of estimation of ordinary distribution function $ F(x); $ they are asymptotical normal still in some rearrangement invariant norm.
nodes.statement_short: For order $\alpha<1/2$ the estimation problem is well posed, with $1/\sqrt{n}$ rate and asymptotic normality.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
assumptions: if the order of the fractional derivative $ \alpha $ is less than 1/2
conclusions: then these problems are well posed

the speed of convergence of offered unbiased estimate is $ 1/\sqrt{n}, $ as in the case of estimation of ordinary distribution function $ F(x); $ they are asymptotical normal still in some rearrangement invariant norm.

nodes.name: Class $K$ of distributions
nodes.statement: In what follows we restrict ourselves by consideration of the following class $ K $ of distributions: $$ \forall F \in K \ \Rightarrow \exists (a,b) \in R^2, \ 0 \le a < b \le \infty, \ F(a+0) = 0, F(b-0) = 1, $$ such that on the interval $ (a,b) $ the function $ F(x) $ is continuous and strictly increasing.
nodes.statement_short: $K$ is the class of distribution functions supported on an interval $(a,b)$ on which $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
differentia: on the interval $ (a,b) $ the function $ F(x) $ is continuous and strictly increasing

nodes.name: Normalization $a = 0$
nodes.statement: We can and will suppose further without loss of generality $ a = 0. $

nodes.name: Fractional derivative of a Rieman-Liouville type
nodes.statement: Let $ \alpha = \const \in (0,1); $ and let $ g = g(x), \ x \in R $ be measurable numerical function. The fractional derivative of a Rieman-Liouville type of order $ \alpha: \ D^{\alpha}[g](x) = g^{(\alpha)}(x) $ is defined as follows: $ \Gamma(1-\alpha) g^{(\alpha)}(x) = $ $$ \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ D^{\alpha}[g](x) = \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x[g](x) \stackrel{def}{= } \frac{d}{dx} \int_0^x \frac{g(t) \ dt}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}. \eqno(1.1) $$
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative of order $\alpha$: differentiate the convolution of $g$ with the kernel $(x-t)^{-\alpha}$, normalized by $\Gamma(1-\alpha)$.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
nodes.definiendum: fractional derivative of a Rieman-Liouville type

nodes.name: Notation for the Gamma function
nodes.statement: Hereafter $ \Gamma(\cdot) $ denotes the ordinary $ \Gamma \ $ function.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Convention: $D^{\alpha}[g](x_0) = 0$ where the derivative fails to exist
nodes.statement: We agree to take $ D^{\alpha}[g](x_0) = 0, $ if at the point $ x_0 $ the expression $ D^{\alpha}[g](x_0) $ does not exists.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Non-locality of the fractional derivative
nodes.statement: Notice that the operator of the fractional derivative is non - local, if $ \alpha $ is not integer non-negative number.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Fractional integral of a Rieman - Liouville type
nodes.statement: Recall also that the fractional integral $ I^{(\alpha)}[\phi](x) = I^{\alpha}[\phi](x) $ of a Rieman - Liouville type of an order $ \alpha, 0 < \alpha < 1 $ is defined as follows: $$ I^{(\alpha)}[\phi](x) \stackrel{def}{=} \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \cdot \int_0^x \frac{\phi(t) \ dt}{(x-t)^{1 - \alpha}}, \ x,t > 0. \eqno(1.1a) $$
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Liouville fractional integral of order $\alpha$: convolution of $\phi$ with the kernel $(x-t)^{\alpha-1}/\Gamma(\alpha)$.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Theorem of Abel
nodes.statement: It is known (theorem of Abel, see \cite{Samko1}, chapter 2, section 2.1) that the operator $ I^{(\alpha)}[\cdot] $ is inverse to the fractional derivative operator $ D^{(\alpha)}[\cdot], $ at least in the class of absolutely continuous functions.
nodes.statement_short: The fractional integral inverts the fractional derivative on absolutely continuous functions.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
nodes.origin_citation: theorem of Abel; Samko, Kilbas & Marichev 1993, chapter 2
assumptions: at least in the class of absolutely continuous functions
conclusions: the operator $ I^{(\alpha)}[\cdot] $ is inverse to the fractional derivative operator $ D^{(\alpha)}[\cdot],

nodes.statement: Note that for the considered further functions this fractional derivative there exists almost everywhere.

nodes.name: Fractional derivative and fractional integral of the indicator $g_h(x) = I(h < x)$
nodes.statement: Let us consider the following important example. Define the function $$ g_h(x) = I(h < x), \ x > 0, \ h = \const > 0. $$ We conclude after simple calculations taking into account our agreement $$ g_h^{(\alpha)}(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \cdot I(h < x) \cdot (x - h)^{-\alpha}, \ \alpha = \const \in (0,1). $$ Let us calculate for the verification the fractional integral $ I^{\alpha} $ of order $ \alpha $ from the function $ x \to g_h^{(\alpha)}(\cdot). $ We have $$ \Gamma(\alpha) \Gamma(1 - \alpha) I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = 0, \ x \le h, $$ and in the case $ x > h $ $$ \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = \int_0^x \frac{I(t > h) \ (t - h)^{-\alpha} \ dt}{ (x - t)^{1 - \alpha}} = $$ $$ \int_h^x (t-h)^{-\alpha} \ (x - t)^{\alpha - 1} \ dt. $$ We make the substitution $$ t = h + y(x-h); \hspace{6mm} dt = (x-h) dy: $$ $$ \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = \int_0^1 y^{ - \alpha} \ (1 - y)^{\alpha - 1} \ dy = $$ $$ B(1 - \alpha, \alpha) = \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) / \Gamma(1) = \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha), $$ where $ B(\cdot, \cdot) $ denotes the usually Beta function. \par Thus, $$ I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = I(h < x) = g_h(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Computes $g_h^{(\alpha)}$ for the indicator $I(h<x)$ and verifies by a Beta-integral substitution that $I^{\alpha}$ recovers $g_h$.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Example is outside the absolutely continuous theory
nodes.statement: Note that since the function $ x \to g_h(x) $ is not absolutely continuous, this result can not be obtained from the results of chapter 2 from the monograph \cite{Samko1}.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Loss functional $\tilde{W}_{n,q}$
nodes.statement: Further, we define as the capacity of a loss function the following $ L_q(R, dF) $ functional $$ \tilde{W}_{n,q} [ D^{\alpha}[F](\cdot), \tilde{F}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[F](x) - \tilde{F}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(1.2) $$ where $ q = \const \ge 1, \ \tilde{F}_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is arbitrary estimation of $ D^{\alpha}[F](\cdot) $ based on our sample.
nodes.statement_short: $\sqrt{n}$-normed $L_q(R,dF)$ risk of an estimate of $D^{\alpha}[F]$.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: "reliability" function $G(x)$
nodes.statement: But it is more convenient sometimes to consider the equivalent problem of estimation of the fractional derivative of so-called "reliability" function $ D^{\alpha}[G](x), $ where $$ G(x) = {\bf P} (\xi_i \ge x) = 1 - F(x), \eqno(1.3) $$ and to take $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) = D^{\alpha}G(x), $
nodes.statement_short: The reliability (survival) function $G(x) = {\bf P}(\xi_i \ge x) = 1 - F(x)$, whose fractional derivative is estimated instead.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Loss functional $W_{n,q}$ for the reliability function
nodes.statement: $$ W_{n,q} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(1.4) $$ where in turn $ \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is arbitrary estimation of $ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) $ based on our sample.
nodes.statement_short: $\sqrt{n}$-normed $L_q(dF)$ risk of an estimate of $D^{\alpha}[G]$.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Relation between $D^{\alpha}[G]$ and $D^{\alpha}[F]$
nodes.statement: Note that $$ D^{\alpha}[1](x) = \frac{x^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha) } \ne 0, $$ so that $$ D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{x^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha) } - D^{\alpha}[F](x) \ne - D^{\alpha}[F](x). \eqno(1.4a) $$
nodes.statement_short: Because $D^{\alpha}[1]\ne 0$, the fractional derivative of $G$ is not simply minus that of $F$.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Empirical approximation of the loss functional
nodes.statement: For the practical using the expression (1.4) may be consistent approximate as $ n \to \infty $ as follows $$ W_q [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \approx \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF_n(x) \right]^{1/q}, $$ where $ F_n(x) $ is ordinary empirical function of distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $dF$ by the empirical $dF_n$ in the risk (1.4) for practical use.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Empirical reliability function $G_n(x)$
nodes.statement: We can define analogously the following estimate of the function $ G(x): $ $$ G_n(x) := n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n I(\xi_i \ge x), \eqno(1.5) $$ empirical reliability function.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Indicator function
nodes.statement: Here $ I(\xi_i \ge x) $ is the usually indicator function: $$ I(\xi_i \ge x) = 1 \ \Leftrightarrow \xi_i \ge x; \hspace{6mm} I(\xi_i \ge x) = 0 \ \Leftrightarrow \xi_i < x. $$
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov's theorem
nodes.statement: Evidently, (Kolmogorov's theorem), the problem of distribution function estimation $ (\alpha = 0) $ is well posed.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
conclusions: the problem of distribution function estimation $ (\alpha = 0) $ is well posed

nodes.name: Konakov's ill-posedness of density estimation
nodes.statement: V.D.Konakov in \cite{Konakov1} proved in contradiction that the problem of density estimation, i.e. when $ \alpha = 1, $ is ill posed.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
conclusions: the problem of density estimation, i.e. when $ \alpha = 1, $ is ill posed

nodes.name: Well posed problem of statistical estimation
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, the result of V.D.Konakov may be reformulated as follows. Certain problem of statistical estimation is well posed iff there exists an estimate (more exactly, a sequence of estimates) such that the speed of convergence is equal (or less than) $ 1/\sqrt{n}. $ As a rule these estimations are asymptotically normal.
nodes.statement_short: A statistical estimation problem is well posed iff some sequence of estimates attains rate $1/\sqrt{n}$ or better.
nodes.section: Notations. Statement of problem.
differentia: there exists an estimate (more exactly, a sequence of estimates) such that the speed of convergence is equal (or less than) $ 1/\sqrt{n}. $

nodes.name: Standing assumptions of the section on point estimation
nodes.statement: {\bf 0.} {\it We suppose in what follows in this section that $ x > 0 $ and } $ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, $ so that $ a = 0, \ 0 < b \le \infty. $
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Indicator $f_h(x) = I(x < h)$
nodes.statement: {\bf 1.} Let us consider the following function $$ x \to f_h(x) = I(x < h), \ h = \const > 0. \eqno(2.1) $$
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Fractional derivative $f_{\alpha,h}$ of the indicator $f_h$
nodes.statement: It is easy to calculate that $$ f_{\alpha,h}(x) := \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ D^{\alpha}[f_h](x) = x^{-\alpha} - (x - h)^{-\alpha} \cdot I(x > h), \ x > 0. \eqno(2.2) $$
nodes.statement_short: Closed form $\Gamma(1-\alpha)D^{\alpha}[f_h](x) = x^{-\alpha} - (x-h)^{-\alpha}I(x>h)$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Estimate $G_{\alpha,n}(x)$ of $D^{\alpha}[G](x)$
nodes.statement: {\bf 2.} It is reasonable to offer as a capacity of the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ at the fixed point $ x, \ x > 0 $ of the fractional derivative $ D^{\alpha}[G](x) $ the following statistic: $$ \Gamma(1-\alpha) \cdot G_{\alpha,n}(x) \stackrel{def}{=} n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x). \eqno(2.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: The proposed estimator is the sample mean of $f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x)$, normalized by $\Gamma(1-\alpha)$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Variance functional $\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)$
nodes.statement: Denote also $$ \Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x) := 2x^{-\alpha} \Gamma(1 - \alpha) G^{(\alpha)}(x) - \Gamma(1 - 2 \alpha) \ G^{(2 \alpha)}(x) - \left(\Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right)^2. \eqno(2.4) $$
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: {\bf A.} Suppose that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) $ there exists. Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is not biased: $$ {\bf E} G_{\alpha,n}(x) = G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.5) $$ \vspace{3mm} {\bf B.} Suppose in addition that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(2 \alpha)}(x) $ there exists. Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is asymptotically as $ n \to \infty $ normal with the variance $$ \Var \left[ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right] = \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)}: \eqno(2.6) $$ \vspace{3mm} $$ \Law \left\{ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right\} \sim N \left(G^{(\alpha)}(x), \ \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)} \right). \eqno(2.7) $$
nodes.statement_short: $G_{\alpha,n}(x)$ is unbiased for $G^{(\alpha)}(x)$ and asymptotically normal with variance $\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)/(n\Gamma^2(1-\alpha))$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.
assumptions: Suppose that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) $ there exists.
Suppose in addition that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(2 \alpha)}(x) $ there exists.
conclusions: Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is not biased: $$ {\bf E} G_{\alpha,n}(x) = G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.5) $$

Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is asymptotically as $ n \to \infty $ normal with the variance $$ \Var \left[ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right] = \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)}: \eqno(2.6) $$ \vspace{3mm} $$ \Law \left\{ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right\} \sim N \left(G^{(\alpha)}(x), \ \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)} \right). \eqno(2.7) $$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to prove the equality (2.5) only for the value $ n = 1. $ We deduce by direct computation using the source definition (1.1) $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot D^{\alpha}_x I(\xi \ge x) \ = \ x^{-\alpha} - (x-\xi)^{-\alpha} \cdot I(\xi < x)= $$ $$ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x), \hspace{6mm} \xi = \xi_1. \eqno(2.8) $$ It remains to take the expectation $ {\bf E} $ from both the sides of the relationship (2.8) to establish the unbiaseness. \par Let us calculate the variance; we consider of course the case $ n = 1. $ $$ \Var := \Var \left[ x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = $$ $$ \Var \left[ (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = S_2 - S_1^2, \eqno(2.9) $$ where $$ S_1 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} \ I(\xi < x) $$ and we know that $$ S_1 = x^{-\alpha} - \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.10) $$ Further, we will use the formula (2.24), section 2, pp. 35-37 from the book \cite{Samko1}: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x [F] = \frac{F(0)}{x^{\alpha}} + \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}} = \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}, $$ since $ F(0) = F(0+) = 0. $ Therefore $$ S_2 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-2 \alpha} \ I(\xi < x) = \int_0^x \frac{d F(t)}{(x-t)^{2 \alpha}} = \Gamma(1 - 2 \alpha) \ D^{2 \alpha}[F](x). \eqno(2.11) $$ It remains to substitute into equality (2.9), taking into account the relation (1.4a). \par The asymptotical normality our estimate follows now from the classical one-dimensional CLT.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation of $D^{\alpha}_x I(\xi \ge x)$ gives unbiasedness; the variance is computed as $S_2 - S_1^2$ using a Samko-Kilbas-Marichev formula, then the classical CLT applies.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Reduce to the case $n = 1$
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to prove the equality (2.5) only for the value $ n = 1. $
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the unbiasedness claim to a single observation.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Direct computation of $D^{\alpha}_x I(\xi \ge x)$
nodes.statement: We deduce by direct computation using the source definition (1.1) $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot D^{\alpha}_x I(\xi \ge x) \ = \ x^{-\alpha} - (x-\xi)^{-\alpha} \cdot I(\xi < x)= $$ $$ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x), \hspace{6mm} \xi = \xi_1. \eqno(2.8) $$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the fractional derivative of the indicator to get $f_{\alpha,\xi}(x)$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Take expectations to obtain unbiasedness
nodes.statement: It remains to take the expectation $ {\bf E} $ from both the sides of the relationship (2.8) to establish the unbiaseness.
nodes.statement_short: Take expectations in (2.8) to conclude unbiasedness.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Decompose the variance as $S_2 - S_1^2$
nodes.statement: Let us calculate the variance; we consider of course the case $ n = 1. $ $$ \Var := \Var \left[ x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = $$ $$ \Var \left[ (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = S_2 - S_1^2, \eqno(2.9) $$ where $$ S_1 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} \ I(\xi < x) $$ and we know that $$ S_1 = x^{-\alpha} - \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.10) $$
nodes.statement_short: Write the variance as $S_2 - S_1^2$ and identify the first moment $S_1$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Compute the second moment $S_2$ via the Samko formula
nodes.statement: Further, we will use the formula (2.24), section 2, pp. 35-37 from the book \cite{Samko1}: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x [F] = \frac{F(0)}{x^{\alpha}} + \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}} = \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}, $$ since $ F(0) = F(0+) = 0. $ Therefore $$ S_2 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-2 \alpha} \ I(\xi < x) = \int_0^x \frac{d F(t)}{(x-t)^{2 \alpha}} = \Gamma(1 - 2 \alpha) \ D^{2 \alpha}[F](x). \eqno(2.11) $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cited integral representation of $D^{\alpha}_x[F]$ to evaluate $S_2$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Substitute into the variance formula
nodes.statement: It remains to substitute into equality (2.9), taking into account the relation (1.4a).
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $S_1, S_2$ back into (2.9) using (1.4a).
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality from the classical CLT
nodes.statement: The asymptotical normality our estimate follows now from the classical one-dimensional CLT.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke the classical one-dimensional CLT for the i.i.d. sum.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Remark 2.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.1.} As follows from the relation (2.8), under condition $ |G^{(\alpha)}(x)| < \infty $ the variable $ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) $ has a finite absolute expectation: $$ {\bf E} |f_{\alpha,\xi} (x)| < \infty. $$ Therefore, on the basis of the Law of Large Numbers, the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is consistent with probability one only under the condition $ |G^{(\alpha)}(x)| < \infty. $
nodes.statement_short: Finite $|G^{(\alpha)}(x)|$ gives an integrable summand, so the LLN yields strong consistency.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Remark 2.2
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.2.} We are not sure that offered in this report estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ of the value $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) $ is optimal, in the contradiction to the Kolmogorov's estimate of the ordinary distribution function.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Remark 2.3
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.3.} Emerging in the theorem 2.1 the variable $ G^{( 2 \alpha)}(x), $ which may be used by the practical application, may be consistent estimated as follows: $$ G^{( 2 \alpha)}(x) \approx G_{2 \alpha,n}(x), $$ as long as $ \alpha < 1/2. $
nodes.statement_short: The unknown $G^{(2\alpha)}(x)$ appearing in the variance can itself be estimated by $G_{2\alpha,n}(x)$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Remark 2.4. Non-asymptotical approach
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.4.} Non-asymptotical approach. \par Let $ x $ be fixed positive number; we consider a non-asymptotical deviation $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_n {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \cdot \left| G_{\alpha,n}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right), \ y \ge 3. \eqno(2.12) $$ Note that the summand r.v. $ f_{\alpha,\xi} = x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha}\cdot I(x > \xi) $ has a heavy tail. Namely, if $$ F(x) - F(0) = F(x) \sim C_1 \ x^{\Delta}, \ x \to 0+, \ \Delta = \const \in (0,1], \ \eqno(2.13) $$ then $$ {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) \sim C_2(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}, \ y \to \infty. \eqno(2.14) $$ The non-asymptotical bounds for $ \sqrt{n} $ normed deviations of sums of these variables are obtained, e.g. the articles \cite{Adler1}, \cite{Bravernan1}, \cite{Bravernan2}, \cite{Ostrovsky3}. We deduce the upper bound for considered probability using these results: $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \le C_3(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha} \ \ln y, \ y > 3. \eqno(2.15) $$ The lower estimate for these probability is trivial: as $ y \to \infty $ $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \ge {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) = C_4(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}(1 + o(1) ). \eqno(2.16) $$ The ultimate value of the degree of the value $ \ln y $ in (2.15) is now unknown.
nodes.statement_short: Non-asymptotic deviation bounds: the summand has a heavy tail $y^{-\Delta/\alpha}$, giving matching-order upper and lower bounds up to a $\ln y$ factor.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Non-asymptotical deviation $P_{\alpha,x}(y)$
nodes.statement: Let $ x $ be fixed positive number; we consider a non-asymptotical deviation $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_n {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \cdot \left| G_{\alpha,n}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right), \ y \ge 3. \eqno(2.12) $$
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Heavy tail of the summand $f_{\alpha,\xi}$
nodes.statement: Note that the summand r.v. $ f_{\alpha,\xi} = x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha}\cdot I(x > \xi) $ has a heavy tail. Namely, if $$ F(x) - F(0) = F(x) \sim C_1 \ x^{\Delta}, \ x \to 0+, \ \Delta = \const \in (0,1], \ \eqno(2.13) $$ then $$ {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) \sim C_2(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}, \ y \to \infty. \eqno(2.14) $$
nodes.statement_short: If $F(x)\sim C_1 x^{\Delta}$ near $0$, the one-observation deviation has a Pareto tail of index $\Delta/\alpha$.

assumptions: F(x) - F(0) = F(x) \sim C_1 \ x^{\Delta}, \ x \to 0+, \ \Delta = \const \in (0,1], \ \eqno(2.13)
conclusions: {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) \sim C_2(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}, \ y \to \infty. \eqno(2.14)

nodes.name: Upper bound for the non-asymptotical deviation
nodes.statement: The non-asymptotical bounds for $ \sqrt{n} $ normed deviations of sums of these variables are obtained, e.g. the articles \cite{Adler1}, \cite{Bravernan1}, \cite{Bravernan2}, \cite{Ostrovsky3}. We deduce the upper bound for considered probability using these results: $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \le C_3(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha} \ \ln y, \ y > 3. \eqno(2.15) $$
nodes.statement_short: $P_{\alpha,x}(y) \le C_3(\alpha,x) y^{-\Delta/\alpha}\ln y$ for $y>3$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.
conclusions: P_{\alpha,x}(y) \le C_3(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha} \ \ln y, \ y > 3. \eqno(2.15)

nodes.name: Lower bound for the non-asymptotical deviation
nodes.statement: The lower estimate for these probability is trivial: as $ y \to \infty $ $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \ge {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) = C_4(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}(1 + o(1) ). \eqno(2.16) $$
nodes.statement_short: Trivially $P_{\alpha,x}(y) \ge C_4(\alpha,x) y^{-\Delta/\alpha}(1+o(1))$.
nodes.section: Point estimate.
conclusions: P_{\alpha,x}(y) \ge {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) = C_4(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}(1 + o(1) ). \eqno(2.16)

nodes.name: Exact power of $\ln y$ in the deviation bound (2.15)
nodes.statement: The ultimate value of the degree of the value $ \ln y $ in (2.15) is now unknown.
nodes.section: Point estimate.

nodes.name: Uniform-norm error estimation is impossible
nodes.statement: As long as the function $ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) $ and correspondingly its estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) $ both are discontinuous and all the more so are unbounded, we can not do the error estimation in the uniform norm, and still can not apply the CLT in the Prokhorov-Skorokhod space, in contradiction to the classical Kolmogorov's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Because $D^{\alpha}[G]$ and its estimate are unbounded and discontinuous, no uniform-norm error bound or Prokhorov-Skorokhod CLT is available.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Loss functional $W_{q,n}$ for the proposed estimate
nodes.statement: We intent to investigate the $ L_q(dF) $ deviation of empirical derivative reliability function $ G_{\alpha,n} $ from its true value $ D^{\alpha}G: \ W_{q,n} :=$ $$ W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \cdot \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - G_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(3.1) $$
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: CLT in $L_q(dF)$ is needed
nodes.statement: As usually, in order to evaluate the variable $ L_q, $ we need to establish the Central Limit Theorem in the Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(dF). $
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Reduction to the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$
nodes.statement: Note first of all that the expression for $ W_q $ in (3.1) does not depend on the function $ F(\cdot) $ inside the set $ K = \{ F \}, $ as in the Kolmogorov's theorem; therefore we can and will suppose $ F(x) = x, 0 \le x \le 1, $ i.e. $ a = 0, b = 1 $ and the r.v. $ \{ \xi_i \} $ have the uniform distribution on the set $ [0,1].$
nodes.statement_short: Since $W_q$ does not depend on $F \in K$, one may take $F(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Covariation kernel $R_{\alpha}(x,y)$
nodes.statement: We introduce some new notations. $ x \cap y := \min(x,y), \ 1 \le q = \const < 1/\alpha, $ $$ R_{\alpha}(x,y) \stackrel{def}{=} \frac{( x \cap y )^{1 - 2 \alpha}}{1 - 2 \alpha} \ - \frac{(x \ y)^{1 - \alpha}}{(1 - \alpha)^2}, \ 0 \le x,y < 1, \ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, \eqno(3.2) $$
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Variance function $\sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)$
nodes.statement: $$ \sigma^2_{\alpha}(x):= R_{\alpha}(x,x) = \frac{ x^{1 - 2 \alpha}}{1 - 2 \alpha} \ - \frac{x^{2 - 2\alpha}}{(1 - \alpha)^2}, $$
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Centering function $g_{\alpha}(x)$
nodes.statement: $$ g_{\alpha}(x) = x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha}, $$
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Normalized empirical process $\zeta_n^{(\alpha)}(x)$
nodes.statement: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(x) = \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ \zeta_n(x) := $$ $$ n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left\{ f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x) - \left[ x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} \right] \right\} = $$ $$ n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left\{ f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x) - g_{\alpha}(x) \right\}, \eqno(3.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta_n^{(\alpha)}$ is the $\sqrt{n}$-normed centered empirical process built from $f_{\alpha,\xi_i}$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Limiting Gaussian process $\zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x)$
nodes.statement: $ \zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x) = \zeta^{(\alpha)}(x) = \zeta(x), \ 0 \le x \le 1 $ be a separable (moreover, continuous with probability one) centered Gaussian random process with covariation function $ R_{\alpha}(x,y): $ \par $$ \Cov(\zeta_{\alpha}(x), \zeta_{\alpha}(y)) = {\bf E} \zeta_{\alpha}(x) \cdot \zeta_{\alpha}(y)= R_{\alpha}(x,y). \eqno(3.4) $$
nodes.statement_short: The limit process is a centered, a.s. continuous Gaussian process with covariance $R_{\alpha}$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Lebesgue-Riesz space $L_q(dF)$
nodes.statement: The ordinary Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(dF) = L_q(R_+,dF) $ consists by definition on all the measurable functions $ f: R_+ \to R $ with finite norms $$ ||f||_q = ||f||L_q(dF) \stackrel{def}{=} \left[ \int_0^{\infty} |f(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \ q = \const \ge 1. $$
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Let $ F(\cdot) \in K $ and let $ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $ Our statement: the sequence of distributions generated in the space $ L_q(dF) $ by the random processes $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ converges weakly as $ n \to \infty $ to the random process $ \zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x) $ (the CLT in the space $ L_q(R_+, dF). $
nodes.statement_short: CLT in $L_q(dF)$: for $q < 1/\alpha$, $\zeta_n^{(\alpha)}$ converges weakly to the Gaussian process $\zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: the sequence of distributions generated in the space $ L_q(dF) $ by the random processes $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ converges weakly as $ n \to \infty $ to the random process $ \zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x) $

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Note first of all that here $$ G^{(\alpha)}(x) = D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[ x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} \right]. \eqno(3.5) $$ as long as in this section $ G(x) = 1 - x, \ x \in (0,1). $ Therefore, all the processes $ \zeta_n(x) $ are centered.\par As before, it is sufficient to consider the centered random process $ \zeta_{1}^{(\alpha)}(x), \ x \in (0,1). $ It is easy to calculate its covariation function; it coincides with $ R_{\alpha}(x,y). $ \par It remains to establish the CLT in the Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(0,1) $ for the sequence $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot). $ The using for us version of CLT in this spaces is obtained, for example, in the fundamental monograph \cite{Ledoux1}, pp. 308-319. Namely, the sufficient condition $$ {\bf E} ||\zeta_1||_q^q < \infty \eqno(3.6) $$ is here satisfied, as long as $ q < 1/\alpha. $ \par In detail, let us denote $$ K(\alpha,q) := \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} < \infty, \eqno(3.7) $$ then $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)| \le \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} + (| (x - \xi)|I(x> \xi)|)^{-\alpha}; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)|^q \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + x^{ - \alpha q } \right]; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q^q = \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ \int_0^1|\zeta_1(x)|^q \ dx \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]; $$ so $$ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q \le \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} = K(\alpha,q) < \infty, \eqno(3.7a) $$ since $ 0 < \alpha < 1, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} This completes the proof of theorem 3.1.
nodes.statement_short: Verify centering and the covariance $R_{\alpha}$, then check the Ledoux-Talagrand sufficient condition ${\bf E}\|\zeta_1\|_q^q<\infty$ by an explicit deterministic bound $K(\alpha,q)$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Compute $G^{(\alpha)}$ and check centering
nodes.statement: Note first of all that here $$ G^{(\alpha)}(x) = D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[ x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} \right]. \eqno(3.5) $$ as long as in this section $ G(x) = 1 - x, \ x \in (0,1). $ Therefore, all the processes $ \zeta_n(x) $ are centered.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $G^{(\alpha)}$ for $G(x)=1-x$ and conclude the processes are centered.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\zeta_1^{(\alpha)}$ and identify its covariance
nodes.statement: As before, it is sufficient to consider the centered random process $ \zeta_{1}^{(\alpha)}(x), \ x \in (0,1). $ It is easy to calculate its covariation function; it coincides with $ R_{\alpha}(x,y). $
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to one observation and check its covariation function equals $R_{\alpha}$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Invoke the CLT in Lebesgue-Riesz spaces
nodes.statement: It remains to establish the CLT in the Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(0,1) $ for the sequence $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot). $ The using for us version of CLT in this spaces is obtained, for example, in the fundamental monograph \cite{Ledoux1}, pp. 308-319. Namely, the sufficient condition $$ {\bf E} ||\zeta_1||_q^q < \infty \eqno(3.6) $$ is here satisfied, as long as $ q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Ledoux-Talagrand version of the CLT, whose sufficient condition is ${\bf E}\|\zeta_1\|_q^q<\infty$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Introduce the constant $K(\alpha,q)$
nodes.statement: In detail, let us denote $$ K(\alpha,q) := \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} < \infty, \eqno(3.7) $$
nodes.statement_short: Define the finite constant $K(\alpha,q)$ that will bound the norm.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Deterministic bound $\|\zeta_1\|_q \le K(\alpha,q)$
nodes.statement: then $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)| \le \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} + (| (x - \xi)|I(x> \xi)|)^{-\alpha}; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)|^q \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + x^{ - \alpha q } \right]; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q^q = \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ \int_0^1|\zeta_1(x)|^q \ dx \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]; $$ so $$ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q \le \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} = K(\alpha,q) < \infty, \eqno(3.7a) $$ since $ 0 < \alpha < 1, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.statement_short: Chain of pointwise and integrated bounds giving $\|\zeta_1\|_q \le K(\alpha,q) < \infty$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: This completes the proof of theorem 3.1.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the proof.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: CLT in Lebesgue-Riesz spaces
nodes.statement: The using for us version of CLT in this spaces is obtained, for example, in the fundamental monograph \cite{Ledoux1}, pp. 308-319. Namely, the sufficient condition $$ {\bf E} ||\zeta_1||_q^q < \infty \eqno(3.6) $$ is here satisfied, as long as $ q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.statement_short: Cited CLT in $L_q$: ${\bf E}\|\zeta_1\|_q^q<\infty$ suffices for weak convergence.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: The using for us version of CLT in this spaces is obtained, for example, in the fundamental monograph \cite{Ledoux1}, pp. 308-319.

nodes.name: Remark 3.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.1.} Note that the obtained estimate (3.7a) is deterministic, i.e. is true still without the expectation {\bf E.}
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Remark 3.2
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.2.} Let us denote $$ Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) = {\bf P} \left( || \zeta_{\alpha}(\cdot)||L_q(0,1) > u \right), \ u = \const > 0. \eqno(3.8) $$ We deduce as a consequence of the theorem 3.1 for the values $ q = \const \in [1, 1/\alpha),\ \alpha \in (0,1/2) $ and $ u > 0 $ $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) = Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u), \eqno(3.9) $$ therefore for sufficiently greatest values $ n $ $$ {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) \approx Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u). \eqno(3.10) $$ The asymptotical behavior of the probability $ Q_{\alpha}(u) $ as $ u \to \infty $ is known, see \cite{Piterbarg1},\cite{Piterbarg2}. Briefly, let us denote $ q' = q/(q - 1), \ q > 1, $ and introduce the variable $$ \beta := \sup_{h: ||h||L(q') = 1} \left\{ \int_0^1 \int_0^1 R_{\alpha}(x,y) h(x) h(y) dx dy \right\}, $$ which may be computed in turn through solving of some non-linear integral equation; then $$ \ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim - \frac{u^2}{2 \beta^2}, \ u \to \infty. $$ The non-asymptotical estimates of this probability is obtained in \cite{Ostrovsky1}, chapter 4, section 4.8; see also \cite{Ostrovsky2}, chapter 3.\par It is clear that the equality (3.10) may be used by construction of confidence region for the unknown function $ G^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm $ L_q(dF) $ and for the testing of non-parametrical hypotheses.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 yields a limiting tail law $Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u)$ that can be used to build $L_q$ confidence regions and test nonparametric hypotheses.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Limiting tail functional $Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u)$
nodes.statement: $$ Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) = {\bf P} \left( || \zeta_{\alpha}(\cdot)||L_q(0,1) > u \right), \ u = \const > 0. \eqno(3.8) $$
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Limiting deviation probability for $G_{\alpha,n}$
nodes.statement: We deduce as a consequence of the theorem 3.1 for the values $ q = \const \in [1, 1/\alpha),\ \alpha \in (0,1/2) $ and $ u > 0 $ $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) = Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u), \eqno(3.9) $$ therefore for sufficiently greatest values $ n $ $$ {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) \approx Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u). \eqno(3.10) $$
nodes.statement_short: The $L_q(dF)$ deviation probability of $G_{\alpha,n}$ converges to $Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u)$, giving an approximation for large $n$.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
assumptions: for the values $ q = \const \in [1, 1/\alpha),\ \alpha \in (0,1/2) $ and $ u > 0 $
conclusions: \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) = Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u), \eqno(3.9)

nodes.name: Logarithmic asymptotics of $Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u)$
nodes.statement: The asymptotical behavior of the probability $ Q_{\alpha}(u) $ as $ u \to \infty $ is known, see \cite{Piterbarg1},\cite{Piterbarg2}. Briefly, let us denote $ q' = q/(q - 1), \ q > 1, $ and introduce the variable $$ \beta := \sup_{h: ||h||L(q') = 1} \left\{ \int_0^1 \int_0^1 R_{\alpha}(x,y) h(x) h(y) dx dy \right\}, $$ which may be computed in turn through solving of some non-linear integral equation; then $$ \ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim - \frac{u^2}{2 \beta^2}, \ u \to \infty. $$
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian-type large deviation: $\ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim -u^2/(2\beta^2)$, with $\beta$ a solution of a nonlinear integral equation.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
assumptions: let us denote $ q' = q/(q - 1), \ q > 1, $
conclusions: \ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim - \frac{u^2}{2 \beta^2}, \ u \to \infty.

nodes.name: Remark 3.3. Verification
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.3. Verification.} It is interest to note that on the case $ \alpha = 0, $ more exactly when $ \alpha \to 0+, $ the obtained before results coincide with the classical belonging to Kolmogorov, Mises etc.
nodes.section: Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Supremal loss $\overline{W}_q$
nodes.statement: We intent to obtain in this section the non-asymptotical {\it upper} estimate for the supremum of loss function $$ \overline{W}_q \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \eqno(4.0) $$
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Supremal deviation probability $\overline{Q}_{\alpha}(u)$
nodes.statement: and as a consequence by means of Tchebychev's inequality the probability $$ \sup_n {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) =: \overline{Q}_{\alpha}(u). \eqno(4.1) $$
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Notations and restrictions retained from section 3
nodes.statement: We retain in this section all the notations and restrictions of third section; for instance, $ F(\cdot) \in K; $ therefore we can and will suppose that the r.v. $ \{ \xi(i) \} $ are independent and uniformly distributed on the set $ [0,1]. $
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Kiefer's exponential bound for the empirical distribution function
nodes.statement: The case $ \alpha = 0, $ i.e. when we consider the classical problem of estimation of ordinary distribution function $ F(x) $ or equally the reliability function $ G(x) = 1 - F(x) $ by means of empirical distribution function $ F_n(x), $ is investigated, and at once in the multidimensional case, even in the uniform norm, i.e. when formally $ q = \infty, $ in the work of J.Kiefer \cite{Kiefer1}; more exact estimate see in the article \cite{Gaivoronsky1}. Indeed, $$ {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \sup_{x} |G_n(x) - G(x)|> u \right) \le 2 e^{- 2 u^2}, \ u \ge 1, \eqno(4.2) $$ i.e. the exponential bound for $ \sqrt{n} $ normed uniform deviation $ \sup_{x} |G_n(x) - G(x)|. $
nodes.statement_short: Classical case $\alpha=0$: ${\bf P}(\sqrt{n}\sup_x|G_n-G|>u)\le 2e^{-2u^2}$.
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \sup_{x} |G_n(x) - G(x)|> u \right) \le 2 e^{- 2 u^2}, \ u \ge 1, \eqno(4.2)

nodes.name: Impossibility of an exponential-tail confidence region for $p \ge 1/\alpha$
nodes.statement: Note first of all that the $ \sqrt{n} $ exponential tail distributed confidence region for $ G^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ based on our estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) $ in the $ L_p $ norm is impossible when $ p \ge 1/\alpha, $ in contradiction to the classical ordinary case $ \alpha = 0. $ Namely, we can deduce the following simple {\it lower } bound for $ \overline{W}_q $ $$ \overline{W}_q \ge W_{q,1} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,1}(\cdot) ], $$ and it is easily to calculate analogously to the relations (3.7) - (3.7a) that $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot {\bf E}|| \left[ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) - G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) \right] ||_q \ge \frac{C_1(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q} }, \ q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(4.3) $$ and $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot {\bf E}|| \left[ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) - G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) \right] ||_q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha, \eqno(4.4) $$
nodes.statement_short: The $L_p$ risk blows up like $(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}$ and is infinite for $q \ge 1/\alpha$, so no exponential-tail confidence region exists there.
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot {\bf E}|| \left[ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) - G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) \right] ||_q \ge \frac{C_1(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q} }, \ q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(4.3)
\Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot {\bf E}|| \left[ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) - G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) \right] ||_q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha, \eqno(4.4)

nodes.name: Restriction $2 \le q < 1/\alpha$
nodes.statement: We are going now to the obtaining of {\it upper} estimates for the value $ \overline{W}_q. $ We suppose in the sequel $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: We propose under formulated above conditions $ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, \ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha $ etc. $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le \frac{C_2(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q}}, \eqno(4.5) $$ where $ C_2(\alpha) $ is continuous positive function on the closed segment $ \alpha \in [0, 1/2]. $
nodes.statement_short: Non-asymptotic bound: $\sup_n W_{q,n} \le C_2(\alpha)(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}/\Gamma(1-\alpha)$.
nodes.section: Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
assumptions: under formulated above conditions $ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, \ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha $ etc.
where $ C_2(\alpha) $ is continuous positive function on the closed segment $ \alpha \in [0, 1/2]. $

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Denote $$ \tau_i(x) = f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x) - {\bf E} f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x), \eqno(4.6) $$ $$ S_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x), \eqno(4.7) $$ then $ \tau_i(x) $ is a sequence of independent identical distributed centered random fields which are proportional with coefficient $ 1/\Gamma(1 - \alpha) $ to the considered before r.f. $ \zeta_i(x). $ \par Let us consider the sequence of random variables $$ V_{\alpha,q}(n) = ||S_n(\cdot)||_q^q = \int_0^1 |S_n(x)|^q \ dx, $$ then we have using Fubini-Tonelli theorem under our condition $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha $ $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) = \int_0^1 {\bf E} |S_n(x)|^q \ dx= \int_0^1 {\bf E} \left| n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x) \right|^q \ dx. \eqno(4.8) $$ We intent to exploit the famous Rosenthal's inequality, see \cite{Rosenthal1}, \cite{Ostrovsky4}. Namely, for arbitrary sequence $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ of independent centered random variables $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot \sqrt{ \sum_{k=1}^n |\zeta_k|_q^2/n }, \hspace{4mm} q \ge 2, \eqno(4.9) $$ where the "Rosenthal's" constant $ K_{R} $ is less than 0.6535, see \cite{Ostrovsky4}. \par If the r.v. $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ are in addition identically distributed, then $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.10) $$ As long as in this section $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha, $ $$ \frac{q}{\ln q} \le \max \left[ \frac{2}{\ln 2}, \ \frac{1/\alpha}{|\ln \alpha|} \right], $$ and if we denote $$ K_{R,\alpha} = K_R \cdot \max \left[ \frac{2}{\ln 2}, \ \frac{1/\alpha}{|\ln \alpha|} \right], \eqno(4.11) $$ then there holds the following inequality (under our conditions) $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R,\alpha} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.12) $$ We conclude after substitution into (4.8) $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) \le K(\alpha,q)^q \cdot K^q_{R,\alpha}. \eqno(4.13) $$ It remains to extract the root of degree $ q $ from last inequality to obtain the estimate $$ \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le K(\alpha,q) \cdot K_{R,\alpha}, $$ which is equivalent to the assertion if theorem 4.1 with explicit evaluate of constant.

nodes.name: Remark 5.2
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 5.2.} I.A.Ibragimov in \cite{Ibragimov1} proved the asymptotical normality of the random process $ \sqrt{n} \left\{I^1[J_n](\lambda) - I^1[F](\lambda) \right\} $ as $ n \to \infty $ in the space $ C(0, 2 \pi) $ of continuous functions. See also \cite{Dahlhaus1}, \cite{Levit1}. A fortiori, the sequence of random processes $$ \zeta_n(\lambda) = \sqrt{n} \cdot \left\{ F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right\} $$ converges weakly in the space $ C(0, 2 \pi) $ as $ n \to \infty $ to the centered separable Gaussian process $ \zeta_{\infty} $ with covariation function $ \Theta_{\alpha}(\lambda, \mu). $ Therefore $$ {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \cdot \max_{\lambda} \left| \left\{ F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right\} \right| > u \right) \approx {\bf P} (\max_{\lambda} | \zeta_{\infty}(\lambda) | > u), \ u = \const > 0. \eqno(5.10) $$ The asymptotical as $ u \to \infty $ behavior of the last probability is fundamental investigated in the monograph \cite{Piterbarg2}, see also \cite{Piterbarg1}: $$ {\bf P} (\max_{\lambda} | \zeta_{\infty}(\lambda) | > u) \sim H(\alpha) \ u^{\kappa - 1} \ \exp \left(-u^2/\sigma^2 \right),\eqno(5.11) $$ $$ H(\alpha), \ \kappa = \const, \ \sigma^2 = \sigma^2(\alpha) = \max_{\lambda \in (0, 2 \pi)} \Theta_{\alpha}(\lambda,\lambda). \eqno(5.11a) $$ The last equalities may be used by construction of confidence region for $ F^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ in the uniform norm. Indeed, let $ 1 - \delta $ be the reliability of confidence region, for example, $ 0.95 $ or $ 0.99 $ etc. Let $ u_0 = u_0(\delta) $ be a maximal root of the equation $$ H(\alpha) \ u_0^{\kappa - 1} \ \exp \left(-u_0^2/\sigma^2 \right) = \delta, $$ then with probability $ \approx 1 - \delta $ $$ \sup_{\lambda \in (0, 2 \pi)} \left| F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right| \le \frac{u_0(\delta)}{\sqrt{n}}. \eqno(5.12) $$

nodes.name: Uniform-norm confidence region for $F^{(\alpha)}$
nodes.statement: The last equalities may be used by construction of confidence region for $ F^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ in the uniform norm. Indeed, let $ 1 - \delta $ be the reliability of confidence region, for example, $ 0.95 $ or $ 0.99 $ etc. Let $ u_0 = u_0(\delta) $ be a maximal root of the equation $$ H(\alpha) \ u_0^{\kappa - 1} \ \exp \left(-u_0^2/\sigma^2 \right) = \delta, $$ then with probability $ \approx 1 - \delta $ $$ \sup_{\lambda \in (0, 2 \pi)} \left| F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right| \le \frac{u_0(\delta)}{\sqrt{n}}. \eqno(5.12) $$
nodes.statement_short: Solving $H(\alpha)u_0^{\kappa-1}e^{-u_0^2/\sigma^2}=\delta$ gives a uniform confidence band of width $u_0(\delta)/\sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Estimation of the fractional derivative of a multidimensional distribution function
nodes.statement: We consider in this section the problem of statistical estimates of fractional derivative for multidimensional distribution function. We restrict ourselves for simplicity only two-dimensional case $ d = 2. $
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Two-dimensional reliability function $G(x,y)$
nodes.statement: In detail, let $ \{ (\xi(i), \eta(i)) \}, i = 1,2,\ldots,n $ be a two dimensional non - negative sample with common distribution function. We define the reliability function $ G = G(x,y) $ as follows: $$ G(x,y) = {\bf P}(\xi(i) \ge x, \ \eta(i) > y), \ x,y \ge 0.\eqno(6.1) $$
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Partial mixed fractional derivative of Rieman-Liouville type
nodes.statement: Let $ \alpha, \beta = \const $ be two numbers such that $ 0 < \alpha, \beta < 1; $ (we will suppose further that $ 0 < \alpha, \beta < 1/2.) $ The partial mixed fractional derivative $ D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) $ again of Rieman-Liouville type of order $ (\alpha, \beta) $ of a function $ G(\cdot, \cdot) $ at the positive points $ (x,y) $ is defined as follows: $$ G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) = D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) \stackrel{def}{=} D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [G] = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \beta)}\times $$ $$ \frac{\partial^2}{ \partial x \partial y } \int_0^x \int_0^y \frac{G(t,s)\ dt \ ds}{ (x-t)^{\alpha} (y-s)^{\beta} }, \eqno(6.2) $$ see, e.g. \cite{Samko1}, chapter 24.
nodes.statement_short: Mixed fractional derivative $D^{\alpha,\beta}_{x,y}[G]$: mixed second partial of the doubly fractional-integrated $G$.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Convention for the undefined mixed fractional derivative
nodes.statement: We put as before $ D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) = 0 $ if at the point (in the plane) $ (x,y) $ the expression (4.2) for $ D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) $ does not exists.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Commutation of mixed fractional derivatives for factorable functions
nodes.statement: Note that in general case $ D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] \ne D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H], $ but if the function $ G = G(x,y) $ is factorable: $ H(x,y) = g_1(x) g_2(y) $ and both the functions $ g_x(\cdot) $ and $ g_2(\cdot) $ are "differentiable" at the points $ x $ and $ y $ correspondingly: $$ \exists D^{\alpha}[g_1](x), \hspace{6mm} \exists D^{\beta}[g_2](y), $$ then really $$ D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H] = D^{\alpha}_x[g_1](x) \cdot D^{\beta}_y [g_2](y). \eqno(6.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: Mixed fractional derivatives commute and factor when $H(x,y)=g_1(x)g_2(y)$ with both factors fractionally differentiable.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.
assumptions: but if the function $ G = G(x,y) $ is factorable: $ H(x,y) = g_1(x) g_2(y) $
conclusions: D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H] = D^{\alpha}_x[g_1](x) \cdot D^{\beta}_y [g_2](y). \eqno(6.3)

nodes.name: Factorable indicator $H(x,y)$ and its mixed derivative
nodes.statement: Introduce as a capacity of the function $ H $ the following: $$ H(x,y) := I(\xi \ge x, \ \eta \ge y), \ \xi = \xi(1), \eta = \eta(1). $$ As long as $$ I(\xi \ge x, \ \eta \ge y) = I(\xi \ge x) \cdot I(\eta \ge y), $$ the function $ H = H(x,y) $ is factorable and therefore (see (6.3)) $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta}(y). \eqno(6.4) $$
nodes.statement_short: For the product indicator $H=I(\xi\ge x)I(\eta\ge y)$ the mixed fractional derivative factors into $f_{\alpha,\xi}(x)f_{\beta,\eta}(y)$.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Two-dimensional estimate $G_{\alpha,\beta,n}(x,y)$
nodes.statement: The consistent with probability one in each fixed point $ (x,y) $ estimate of the function $ G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) $ is follows: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) G_{\alpha, \beta,n }(x,y) \stackrel{def}{=} n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta(i)}(y). \eqno(6.5) $$
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Properties of the two-dimensional estimate
nodes.statement: It is easily to verify that the estimate $ G_{\alpha, \beta,n }(x,y) $ obeys at the same properties as its one-dimensional predecessor $ G_{\alpha, n }(x), $ for example, is unbiased, satisfies LLN and CLT.
nodes.statement_short: The bivariate estimate inherits unbiasedness, the LLN and the CLT from the one-dimensional case.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.
conclusions: obeys at the same properties as its one-dimensional predecessor $ G_{\alpha, n }(x), $ for example, is unbiased, satisfies LLN and CLT.

nodes.name: Product field $h_{\alpha,\beta}(x,y)$
nodes.statement: $$ h_{\alpha, \beta}(x,y) = h_{\alpha, \beta}(\xi, \eta; x,y) := f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta}(y), \ \xi = \xi(1), \eta = \eta(1)\eqno(6.6) $$
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Factorability without independence
nodes.statement: Note that despite the function $$ h_{\alpha, \beta}(x,y) = h_{\alpha, \beta}(\xi, \eta; x,y) := f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta}(y), \ \xi = \xi(1), \eta = \eta(1)\eqno(6.6) $$ is also factorable, we do not suppose the independence of the r.v. $ (\xi, \eta). $
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Two-dimensional normed sum $S_n(x,y)$
nodes.statement: Define as before the following sequence of random fields $$ S_n(x,y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( h_{\alpha, \beta}(\xi(i), \eta(i); x,y) - \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) \right), \eqno(6.7) $$ so that $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) \left[ G_{(\alpha, \beta,n)}(x,y) - G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) \right] = n^{-1/2} S_n(x,y). \eqno(6.8) $$
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Norm asymptotics of $h_{\alpha,\beta}$
nodes.statement: Further, it is clear that $$ || h_{\alpha, \beta}(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q,X; r,Y} \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q} \ (1 - \beta r)^{-1/r}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, 1 \le r < 1/\beta. \eqno(6.9) $$
nodes.statement_short: The mixed-norm of $h_{\alpha,\beta}$ behaves like $(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}(1-\beta r)^{-1/r}$.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.
conclusions: || h_{\alpha, \beta}(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q,X; r,Y} \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q} \ (1 - \beta r)^{-1/r},

nodes.name: Non-mixed case $r = q \ge 2$ and the two variants
nodes.statement: Let return to the source problem and let us consider only the non-mixed case $ r = q; $ then $$ ||h(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q,q} = ||h(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q, F} = \left[\int_X \int_Y |h(x,y)|^q F(dx,dy) \right]^{1/q}.\eqno(6.10) $$ Assume also $ q \ge 2, $ so $ 2 \le q = r < \min(1/\alpha, 1/\beta). $\par We will distinguish two essentially different variants: $ V_1: \beta < \alpha $ and $ V_2: \beta = \alpha. $ The case $ \beta > \alpha $ may be considered analogously.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to $r=q\ge 2$ below $\min(1/\alpha,1/\beta)$ and split into the variants $\beta<\alpha$ and $\beta=\alpha$.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: First possibility: $\beta < \alpha$
nodes.statement: {\bf First possibility:} $ \beta < \alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} We find after simple calculations as in fourth section using Rosenthal's inequality: $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_1(\alpha, \beta, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-1}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.11) $$ and $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.11a) $$
nodes.statement_short: For $\beta<\alpha$, $\sup_n {\bf E}\|S_n\|_{q,F}^q \asymp C_1 (1-\alpha q)^{-1}$, and is infinite once $q \ge 1/\alpha$.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.
conclusions: \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_1(\alpha, \beta, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-1}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.11)
\sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.11a)

nodes.name: Second possibility: $\beta = \alpha$
nodes.statement: {\bf Second possibility:} $ \beta = \alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} We have analogously $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_2(\alpha, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-2}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.12) $$ and $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.12a) $$
nodes.statement_short: For $\beta=\alpha$ the blow-up is squared: $\asymp C_2 (1-\alpha q)^{-2}$, infinite for $q \ge 1/\alpha$.
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.
conclusions: \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_2(\alpha, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-2}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.12)
\sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.12a)

nodes.name: CLT criterion for the two-dimensional fields
nodes.statement: As a consequence: the sequence of r.f. $ S_n(\cdot, \cdot) $ in both the considered cases satisfies the CLT in the space $ L_q(F(dx, dy)) $ iff $ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.
conclusions: the sequence of r.f. $ S_n(\cdot, \cdot) $ in both the considered cases satisfies the CLT in the space $ L_q(F(dx, dy)) $ iff $ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $

nodes.name: Confidence regions in the multivariate case
nodes.statement: Thus, there is a possibility to built the asymptotical and non-asymptotical confidence region for estimated mixed fractional derivative $ F^{(\alpha, \beta)}(\cdot, \cdot), \ \alpha, \beta < 1/2 $ still in the multivariate case in the $ L_q(dF) $ norm as well as in the fixed point $ (x_0, y_0). $
nodes.section: Multidimensional case.

nodes.name: Grand Lebesgue Space (GLS) $G\psi$
nodes.statement: Let $ (X, M, \mu ) $ be a probability space with non-trivial probability measure $ \mu, $ and let also $ \psi = \psi(q), \ 1 \le q < s, \ s = \const \in (1, \infty] $ be continuous on the open interval $ ( 1, s ) $ bounded from below function. By definition, a Grand Lebesgue Space (GLS) $ G\psi $ over our triplet $ (X, M, \mu ) $ consists on all the measurable functions $ f: X \to R $ with finite norm $$ ||f||G\psi \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_{q \in (1,s)} \left[ \frac{|f|_q}{\psi(q)} \right]. \eqno(7.1) $$ Hereafter $$ |f|_q = \left[ \int_X |f(x)|^q \ \mu(dx) \right]^{1/q} $$ and we will denote $ s = \supp \psi. $
nodes.statement_short: $G\psi$ collects measurable $f$ whose $L_q$ norms, rescaled by $\psi(q)$, stay bounded over $q \in (1,s)$.
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.
nodes.origin_citation: Fiorenza; Iwaniec & Sbordone; Kozachenko & Ostrovsky; Ostrovsky & Sirota
nodes.genus: all the measurable functions $ f: X \to R $

nodes.name: Setting for the Grand Lebesgue Space estimate
nodes.statement: We choose supposing without loss of generality $ a = 0, \ b = 1, $ so that $ \dim \xi = 1 $ and $ F(0+) = 0, \ F(1 - 0) = 1, \ F \in K, \ \alpha \in (0,1/2), $ $$ X = [0,1] \otimes \Omega, $$ so that the measure $ \mu $ is direct product of ordinary Lebesgue measure $ dx $ and probability measure $ P: $ $$ \mu(A \otimes B) = \int_A dx \cdot {\bf P}(B), \ A \subset [0,1], \ B \subset \Omega, \eqno(7.2) $$ where $ \Omega = \{ \omega \} $ is source probability space, i.e. in which is defined our sample $ \{ \xi(i) \}. $
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Proposition 7.1
nodes.statement: $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,\omega): |S_n(x)| > u \} \le C_3(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: Uniform tail bound $\sup_n \mu\{|S_n|>u\} \le C_3(\alpha)u^{-\alpha}\ln u$ for $u \ge e$.
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.
conclusions: \sup_n \mu \{ (x,\omega): |S_n(x)| > u \} \le C_3(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.3)

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.1
nodes.statement: Put $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) = (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$ Note that $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-\alpha}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$ The assertion (4.5) may be rewritten as follows. $$ \sup_n | S_n(\cdot, \cdot) |_{q, \mu} \le C_4(\alpha) \ \psi_{\alpha}(q), \eqno(7.4) $$ or equally on the language of the Grand Lebesgue Spaces $$ \sup_n || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||G\psi_{\alpha} \le C_4(\alpha) < \infty. \eqno(7.5) $$ The tail estimate (7.3) follows immediately from one of results of the article \cite{Ostrovsky7}; see also \cite{Ostrovsky8}.
nodes.statement_short: Recast the moment bound (4.5) as a Grand Lebesgue Space norm bound for $\psi_{\alpha}(q)=(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}$, then quote the GLS tail estimate.
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Introduce the generating function $\psi_{\alpha}(q)$
nodes.statement: Put $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) = (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$ Note that $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-\alpha}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi_{\alpha}(q)$ and note its equivalent form.
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Rewrite Theorem 4.1 as a GLS norm bound
nodes.statement: The assertion (4.5) may be rewritten as follows. $$ \sup_n | S_n(\cdot, \cdot) |_{q, \mu} \le C_4(\alpha) \ \psi_{\alpha}(q), \eqno(7.4) $$ or equally on the language of the Grand Lebesgue Spaces $$ \sup_n || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||G\psi_{\alpha} \le C_4(\alpha) < \infty. \eqno(7.5) $$
nodes.statement_short: Restate (4.5) as $\sup_n \|S_n\|G\psi_{\alpha} \le C_4(\alpha)$.
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Quote the GLS tail estimate
nodes.statement: The tail estimate (7.3) follows immediately from one of results of the article \cite{Ostrovsky7}; see also \cite{Ostrovsky8}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cited GLS-norm-to-tail result to conclude (7.3).

nodes.name: Remark 7.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 7.1.} It is not hard to generalize this result into the multidimensional case described in the $ 6^{th} $ section. Namely, if in the notations of the $ 6^{th} $ section $ 0 < \beta < \alpha < 1/2, $ then $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,y, \omega): |S_n(x,y)| > u \} \le C_5(\alpha, \beta) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e; \eqno(7.6) $$ if $ 0 < \beta = \alpha < 1/2, $ then $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,y, \omega): |S_n(x,y)| > u \} \le C_6(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln^2 u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.7) $$
nodes.statement_short: The tail bound extends to the two-dimensional setting, with an extra $\ln u$ factor when $\beta = \alpha$.
nodes.section: Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Weight case
nodes.statement: Perhaps, it is interest to investigate the error of the approximation of a form $$ V(x) \cdot ( W \cdot F)^{(\alpha)}(x) \approx V(x) \cdot ( W \cdot F)_{n,\alpha}(x), $$ or analogously $$ V(x) \cdot ( W * F)^{(\alpha)}(x) \approx V(x) \cdot ( W * F)_{n,\alpha}(x), $$ or analogously $$ V(x) * ( W * F)^{(\alpha)}(x) \approx V(x) *( W * F)_{n,\alpha}(x), $$ where $ V(x), W(x) $ are two weight functions, for instance, $ V(x) = |x|^{\gamma}, \ W(x) = |x|^{\Delta}, \hspace{6mm} \gamma, \Delta = \const. $
nodes.statement_short: Open: error analysis for weighted (multiplicative or convolutional) versions of the fractional-derivative approximation.
nodes.section: Concluding remarks.

nodes.name: Semi-parametric case
nodes.statement: Let $ \xi(i), \ i = 1,2,\ldots,n $ be a sample of a volume $ n $ with parametric family of regular distribution of a form $$ {\bf P} (\xi(i) < x) = F(x; \theta), $$ where $ \theta \in \Theta \subset R^k, \ k < \infty $ is (multidimensional, in general case) unknown numerical parameter. \par Denote by $ \hat{\theta}_n $ the maximum likelihood estimate of the parameter $ \theta $ builded on our sample. The asymptotical tail behavior of distribution for the following statistic $$ \tau_n := \sqrt{n} \cdot || F(\cdot, \hat{\theta}_n ) - F_n(\cdot) ||L, $$ where $ || \cdot||L $ is some Banach functional norm in the space $ x \in R, $ is in detail investigated in \cite{Piterbarg1}, \cite{Piterbarg2}, chapter 5.\par By our opinion, it is interest to obtain also the asymptotical tail behavior of the following statistic $$ \tau_{n,\alpha} := \sqrt{n} \cdot || F^{(\alpha)}(\cdot, \hat{\theta}_n ) - F_{n,\alpha}(\cdot) ||L, $$ $ \alpha = \const \in (0, 1/2). $
nodes.statement_short: Open: asymptotic tail behaviour of $\tau_{n,\alpha}$, the fractional-derivative analogue of the classical semi-parametric goodness-of-fit statistic.
nodes.section: Concluding remarks.

nodes.name: Applications (possible) in statistics
nodes.statement: The asymptotical tail behavior of the statistic $ \tau_{n,\alpha} $ may be used perhaps in turn in statistics, for instance, for the verification of semi-parametrical hypotheses and detection of distortion times etc.
nodes.section: Concluding remarks.
